clue.text: Some matter for the press.

parts.note: printers and editors call the text that is sent to be set and printed by this name

explanation.definitionFit: Journalists use the word for written material ready for typesetting, so it is literally matter handed to the press.

clue.text: Take in.

parts.note: to take something in is to grasp it with the mind, though the phrase also suggests deceiving or admitting

explanation.definitionFit: Taking in an idea means understanding it fully, the mental grasp the answer names.

clue.text: It's just fawning, Dad and the artists it in charge!

parts.note: Pa is a familiar word for a father
RAs are Royal Academicians, members of London's Royal Academy of Arts, so artists in the plural give RAS
taken as written

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry that all this sucking up, by father and the painters alike, is just fawning on whoever holds power.
explanation.definitionFit: A hanger-on who lives off a patron behaves in a sycophantic, sponging way, which is fawning conduct.

clue.text: Put on show in red-that's what!

definitions.text: Put on show in red-that's what!

indicators.note: the staging verb sits inside the colour word, so in signals one piece placed within another

parts.note: taken as written
to put on a show, a play or film, is to stage or mount it

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a show being staged all over again, this time in red.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's what!' only links; read as a whole, the clue describes a show staged a second time, which is what the answer means.
explanation.definitionFit: Something staged a second time has been mounted anew, a copied or repeated production.

clue.text: They appear in storied bust (not urn)!

indicators.note: bust means broken, so the letters of the word storied are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: A joke about sculpture: these people turn up in a bust carved with stories, not on an urn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' looks like a piece of sculpture (hence the aside about an urn) but signals the anagram of STORIED; 'appear in' and the bracket are surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The people who appear in newspaper stories as their shapers are the journalists who correct and prepare copy.

clue.text: Properly fed up.

parts.note: fed up usually means bored or annoyed, but read literally it means filled with food, and properly means fully so

explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has eaten their fill is sated and stuffed, filled up by food in the literal sense.

clue.text: Ten dined — costly perhaps-yet not in a happy way.

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the words ten, dined and costly may be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: Ten people had an expensive dinner yet came away grumbling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals an anagram of TEN DINED COSTLY, all fourteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting with dissatisfaction or grumbling resentment is behaving unhappily.

clue.text: Where it should be easy to spot a treble.

definitions.text: Where it should be easy to spot a treble.

parts.words: Where it should be easy to spot a treble.
parts.note: a treble sounds like a triple or a drink, but here it is a boy soprano, found among church singers

explanation.definitionFit: A treble is a high boy's voice, and church singing groups are full of them.

clue.text: The last thing one would want to bite.

definitions.text: The last thing one would want to bite.

parts.words: The last thing one would want to bite.
parts.note: the idiom of biting the earth's powder means falling dead, so nobody wants to bite it

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for dying is to bite fine powdery dirt, so that dirt is the last thing anyone wants between their teeth.

clue.text: State of the china after the bull's call

definitions.text: State of the china after the bull's call

parts.words: State of the china after the bull's call
parts.note: the proverbial bull in a china shop leaves the crockery scattered everywhere, and the idiom means in total disorder

explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for widely scattered or in complete disarray, pictured here as smashed crockery strewn across the store.

clue.text: Let us be ——. Let us contemplate existence," said Mr Pecksniff.

definitions.text: Let us be ——. Let us contemplate existence," said Mr Pecksniff.

parts.words: Let us be ——. Let us contemplate existence," said Mr Pecksniff.
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit, where the hypocrite Pecksniff preaches righteousness

explanation.definitionFit: Pecksniff, Dickens's sanctimonious hypocrite, urges his hearers to be virtuous and ethical, the word missing from his speech.

clue.text: Triumph and Disaster were two Kipling.

definitions.text: Triumph and Disaster were two Kipling.

parts.words: Triumph and Disaster were two Kipling.
parts.note: Kipling's poem If tells the reader to meet Triumph and Disaster and treat those two frauds just the same

explanation.definitionFit: In Kipling's poem If, triumph and disaster are called two deceivers, frauds pretending to be what they are not.

definitions.meaning: literally, having eyes shining like stars

definitions.text: rather out of touch with life

explanation.definitionFit: The compound means literally having sparkling eyes and figuratively naive and dreamy, idealistic beyond reality.

clue.text: Appeal from a centre at least a yard

indicators.note: from shows the answer is taken out of the run of letters in the following words

explanation.surface: A plea made from somewhere central, keeping at least a yard of distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' signals the letters concealed in cENTRE AT; the rest of the surface is padding.
explanation.definitionFit: To plead with someone earnestly is to beg or beseech them, making an earnest request.

clue.text: Delights renascent in another guise

indicators.note: a new guise is a new appearance, so the letters of renascent are dressed in a different order

explanation.surface: Joys that are reborn in a different form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in another guise' signals an anagram of RENASCENT; 'Delights' is a verb here, as in charms.
explanation.definitionFit: To enchant someone is to charm or captivate them, which is what delights does as a verb.

clue.text: This may be indicative of an old learning.

definitions.text: This may be indicative of an old learning.

parts.words: This may be indicative of an old learning.
parts.note: a striped neck accessory in British school colours, the old school tie, signals where someone was educated

explanation.definitionFit: The British old school tie is a strip of cloth knotted at the collar whose stripes reveal the wearer's former school.

clue.text: Once twenty shillings? This means comment.

parts.note: ex means former, so once gives EX
in old British money there were twenty shillings to the pound

explanation.surface: A question about old money, followed by the claim that it amounts to commentary.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 the British pound was divided into twenty shillings.
explanation.definitionFit: To set out or explain a text at length is to comment on it in detail.

clue.text: No rates for him maybe, despite his position.

definitions.text: No rates for him maybe, despite his position.

indicators.note: maybe suggests the words no rates might be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: A grumble that a public figure escapes local taxes despite his rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' signals the anagram of NO RATES; rates were British local property taxes.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a legislative upper house holds high office yet, as the anagram says, pays no rates.

clue.text: Like that triangular affair in which the-sides aren't equal.

definitions.text: Like that triangular affair in which the-sides aren't equal.

parts.words: Like that triangular affair in which the-sides aren't equal.
parts.note: a love triangle is suggested, but the geometry term for a triangle with three unequal sides is meant

explanation.definitionFit: Geometry names a triangle whose three sides all differ in length with this term.

parts.note: nor means and not
Ma is a familiar word for a mother

explanation.surface: A child's complaint that the family excludes Mother, as is usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as a' only links; Latin norma, a carpenter's square, is a standard or rule.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for a carpenter's square, the word means a standard or pattern, a rule to measure by.

clue.text: A sheepish lot, these females.

parts.note: sheepish usually means bashful, but here it means literally of sheep, female ones

explanation.definitionFit: Female sheep have their own name, so a flock of them is literally a sheepish band of females.

definitions.text: What a rising star may well prove.

parts.words: What a rising star may well prove.
parts.note: a rising star sounds like an up-and-coming celebrity, but a star in astrology brings good fortune

explanation.definitionFit: One's fortunate star in the heavens brings good luck, so a rising star may prove fortunate.
